paper_title: MARGIN: Runtime Confidence Calibration for Multi-Agent Foundation Model Coordination

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When a coordinator compares answers from heterogeneous foundation models, self-reported confidence may have different meanings across responders and changing workloads. This paper presents MARGIN (Multi-Agent Runtime Grading via Incremental Normalisation), a runtime calibration method that learns model-specific confidence corrections from observed answer outcomes without retraining the models or requiring a held-out calibration set. MARGIN tracks recent accuracy and stated confidence within confidence bands, uses their ratio to correct reported confidence, and blends sparse-band corrections toward a model-level estimate. The corrected scores weight candidate answers in a collective decision. Evaluation covers code generation, question answering, and mathematics, using an 18-model pool and a nine-model subset for distribution-shift experiments. On BigCodeBench, model-mean confidence is negatively related to accuracy; among correct/incorrect response pairs, choosing the more confident responder performs below chance. Against five online calibration baselines receiving identical feedback and retaining their learned state across each transition, MARGIN achieves lower post-shift expected calibration error than all five in two code-generation transitions and than four in a question-answering transition; the remaining question-answering comparison is inconclusive. In separate code-generation coordination experiments, calibration improves the ranking of correct responses and increases answer-selection accuracy by 4.3 and 14.0 percentage points on two of three benchmarks relative to uncalibrated confidence weighting. These results support model-specific runtime calibration for coordination under changing workloads when correctness feedback is available for the participating responders.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A coordinator combining answers from heterogeneous foundation models must decide how much weight to give each response. Self-reported confidence provides an immediate signal, but the same numerical score can mean different things for different models. For example, responder claiming 90% confidence may be less reliable than one claiming 70%. Language-model confidence is often miscalibrated [11, 37]; when those scores are used to compare or aggregate answers, miscalibration becomes coordination problem rather than just an individual-model diagnostic. Changing workloads introduce second difficulty. confidence correction describes the relationship between stated confidence and correctness on the tasks encountered. When the task distribution changes, correction learned from earlier outcomes may no longer be appropriate. This 1 can happen without changing the models themselves: the questions change while their weights and response policies remain fixed. confidence-based coordinator therefore needs both model-specific corrections and way to revise them as new evidence arrives. Fixed post-hoc methods, including temperature scaling, Platt scaling, and histogram binning, fit corrections on calibration data [14, 27, 29]. Their performance can deteriorate under distribution shift [28]. Online calibration instead updates from subsequent outcomes [7, 10]. MARGIN operates in this online setting alongside the histogram, windowed-accuracy, and online Platt methods evaluated here. The relevant comparison is between correction rules that receive the same feedback and must adapt calibration learned on an earlier workload to changed task distribution. MARGIN maintains exponentially weighted estimates of accuracy and stated confidence within each models confidence bands. Their ratio discounts or increases reported confidence according to observed reliability. Separate bands allow confidence-dependent corrections; within-model shrinkage shares information when band has few observations; and exponential weighting reduces the influence of older outcomes. The calibrated scores then weight candidate answers in collective vote. The construction uses only model outputs, stated confidence, and subsequent correctness feedback, without model internals, retraining, or separate calibration dataset. The evaluation separates adaptation after workload change from calibration started without prior history. For each shift, all online methods receive the same source observations and outcomes, retain their state at the transition, and continue updating on the target workload. MARGIN has lower post-shift expected calibration error (ECE) than all five online baselines in two code-generation transitions and than four of five in question-answering transition. The remaining question-answering comparison is inconclusive. Mathematics and same-task test-hardening conditions complete the shift evaluation. Single-benchmark experiments separately assess performance without prior calibration history, while selected-model-feedback diagnostic tests the dependence on observing outcomes for the whole responding pool. Separate coordination experiments establish the downstream relevance of calibration. MARGIN improves the ranking of correct responses on the three evaluated code-generation benchmarks and answer-selection accuracy on two. Previous evaluations have found that verbalized confidence can poorly distinguish correct from incorrect answers, including below-chance discrimination in some modeltask settings [37]. Our BigCodeBench evaluation identifies confidence inversion across the heterogeneous pool: model-mean confidence is negatively associated with accuracy, and among pairs containing one correct and one incorrect response to the same task, choosing the more confident responder performs below random choice before calibration (Section 7.3). The matched-feedback shift experiments then assess how alternative online corrections adapt when the workload changes. The contributions are: (i) confidence-band runtime calibration mechanism for heterogeneous model coordination; (ii) comparative evidence on adaptation after task-distribution changes, with online alternatives given the same feedback and retained histories; and (iii) an empirical diagnosis of confidence inversion on BigCodeBench, with evaluations of pairwise recovery, answer selection, and feedback requirements. stationary estimator analysis explains the bias introduced by asymmetric success/failure updates. Calibration and coordination performance are established by the experiments.

sections.content: Consider pool of foundation-model responders = {a1, . . . , aN } and sequence of tasks qt. For each task, participating subset At produces answers ˆyi,t and stated confidences ci,t [0, 1]. coordinator receives these outputs and selects an answer. Subsequently, task-specific evaluator 2 may supply the correctness outcome oi,t {0, 1}. For code generation, executable tests determine this outcome, so correct program need not match reference solution. The coordinator learns time-dependent correction fi,t for each responder. Its calibration objective is Pr(oi,t = 1 ci,t = p) p, ci,t = fi,t(ci,t), (1) where fi,t uses only outcomes available before scoring task t. The objective is assessed on the observed stream; it is not an assumption that changing workloads are already calibrated. The corrected confidence also supplies weight for answer-level aggregation. This is coordinator/responder setting within multi-agent systems. An agent here is model instance participating in the pool. The evaluated responders independently answer each task, retain no inter-task state, and do not receive the coordinators calibration state as feedback. MARGIN changes only how the coordinator interprets their confidence, and their response policies stay fixed. No model weights, logits, or training data are available to the coordinator, and no held-out calibration set is used. The primary experiments provide correctness feedback for every usable response after scoring. Section 7.5 separately examines diagnostic in which only the responder with the highest calibrated confidence receives an update. Interactive deliberation, planning, strategic adaptation, and trajectory-dependent confidence are outside the evaluated setting.

sections.title: 3.1 Calibration and Online Adaptation
sections.content: Post-hoc calibration fits mapping from prediction scores to empirical correctness. Temperature scaling adjusts the sharpness of model distribution, Platt scaling fits logistic correction, and histogram methods estimate correctness within score regions [14, 27, 29]. When these corrections are fitted once and held fixed, their validity depends on the relationship between the calibration and deployment distributions. Ovadia et al. [28] demonstrate the importance of evaluating uncertainty under dataset shift rather than extrapolating from in-distribution calibration. Large language model (LLM) calibration also addresses transfer and the cost of obtaining suitable supervision. Thermometer learns an auxiliary calibrator from multiple tasks for use on new tasks [31]. ConfTuner fine-tunes verbalized confidence using tokenized Brier-score objective [23]. Luo et al. [26] use pre-trained reference model to calibrate post-trained model without labelled calibration data, restricting confidence alignment to examples where their predictions agree. These approaches differ in their access and training requirements. MARGIN keeps the responding models fixed and updates the coordinators correction from observed answer outcomes. Sequential calibration studies probabilities that are evaluated and revised as outcomes arrive [7, 10]. Prediction with expert advice uses successive losses to allocate weight among predictors [3]; multicalibration requires calibration across specified, potentially overlapping groups [15]. These address related but distinct objectives. MARGIN uses fixed model/confidence-band groups and evaluates both their probability correction and its consequences for answer selection. Its estimator theorem concerns update bias and makes no claim about regret or multicalibration. Adaptive conformal inference instead adapts coverage criterion under shift [13], which is different from the point-confidence objective here. The direct empirical comparison is with online histogram, windowed-accuracy, and logistic calibration rules specified in Section 6.2. They receive the same observations and retain their own source state when the workload changes. This comparison assesses the combined ratio, banding, and 3 shrinkage construction against alternative update rules. Exponential weighting itself is established estimation machinery [18, 30].

sections.title: 3.2 Confidence Signals and Model Selection
sections.content: Confidence elicitation determines the signal available to coordinator; calibration determines how to interpret that signal against outcomes. Tian et al. [33] study direct requests for verbalized probabilities. Xiong et al. [37] compare confidence-elicitation strategies and report that vanilla verbalized confidence can have poor failure-detection performance, including below-chance point estimates in some settings. Their analysis ranks different answers produced by an individual model. Our pairwise diagnostic compares responders answering the same task; separate statistic measures the association between models mean confidence and accuracy. The measurements are related without being interchangeable. Other approaches derive confidence from repeated responses. Self-consistency samples reasoning paths and aggregates their answers [34]; semantic uncertainty groups meaning-equivalent responses rather than treating every different string as distinct answer [9, 21]. Surveys organise the wider set of confidence-estimation and calibration approaches [11, 25]. MARGINs primary evaluation uses verbalized confidence, while matched agreement-based signals are sensitivity evidence. Its runtime correction acts on the supplied signal rather than changing the elicitation procedure. Confidence-based model selection and cost-aware cascades make different decisions about model use. Gerych et al. [12] predict confidence for modelprompt pairs with an auxiliary regressor to select pair for each query. FrugalGPT learns cascades that trade answer quality against modelquery cost [4]. Here the candidate responses have already been obtained: MARGIN weights their contributions to the final answer. The experiments assess this post-response coordination layer. Savings from choosing which model to query are separate question.

sections.title: 3.3 Multi-Agent Coordination and Trust
sections.content: Foundation-model multi-agent systems employ debate, delegation, and structured conversation [8, 32, 36, 38]. In those settings, interaction can alter the answers that agents eventually provide. The relationship between such systems and classical agent models is discussed by La Malfa et al. [22]. MARGIN studies the confidence-bearing interface between independent responders and coordinator. The respondents policies remain fixed; what changes is the coordinators interpretation of their reported confidence. Trust and reputation methods likewise use evidence about participants to guide subsequent decisions. Jøsang et al. [19] survey their varied formulations and evidence sources. EigenTrust, for example, aggregates transaction-based ratings into global reputation value for each peer [20]. single participant-level score can hide differences between confidence regions: the same responder may be reliable when reporting moderate confidence yet overstate its reliability at high confidence. MARGIN tracks this particular context explicitly through model/confidence-band state. Its multiplicative factor describes how reported score should be adjusted, rather than serving as an unconditional ranking of agents. This connects the method to outcome-based trust while keeping the evaluated information contract concrete: candidate answers, stated confidence, and later correctness feedback. The selectedmodel-feedback diagnostic tests what happens when the coordinator observes outcomes only for the responder it chooses, thereby concentrating the evidence used for future calibration.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: MARGIN estimates how much responders stated confidence should be corrected within each confidence region. Two exponentially weighted moving averages (EWMAs) track observed accuracy and stated confidence. Their ratio supplies the correction, within-model shrinkage stabilises sparsely observed bands, and the corrected scores enter an answer-level vote.

sections.title: 6.1 Workloads, Cohorts, and Evaluation Design
sections.content: The experiments ask two questions: how well does calibration adapt after the workload changes, and how useful are the corrected scores for choosing an answer? The first is evaluated on sourceto-target transitions. The second is evaluated separately by replaying answer selection within benchmark from an initially empty calibration history, referred to below as cold start. source phase provides previous calibration experience. No method is tuned on it as held-out dataset. Code-generation tasks provide correctness labels through execution. HumanEval (HE) [5] and Mostly Basic Python Problems (MBPP) [1] supply the two source workloads; the hard subset of BigCodeBench (BCB) [39] is the coding target. HumanEval+ and MBPP+ use expanded tests from EvalPlus [24] on the original candidate programs. These two hardening checks change the correctness criterion for previously seen tasks; they are not independent unseen-question generalisation tests. The question-answering transition (MMLU-shift) moves from science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) questions in Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) [16] to business questions in MMLU-Pro [35]. The latter introduces harder questions and up to ten answer options; benchmark, subject, and format change together. Mathematics shifts from grade-school problems in GSM8K [6] to competition problems in MATH [17]. Table 1 summarises retained task support. Appendix gives the model inventory, prompts, scoring support, and exact comparison protocols. The canonical pool contains 18 models1: nine cloud-served models from the Qwen, DeepSeek, 1Gemma-4-31B-it was also collected but is excluded from the canonical cohort. It belongs to later model 8 GPT-OSS, MiniMax, and GLM families, and nine locally served Qwen, LLaMA, Phi, DeepSeek Coder, and Mistral variants. Cold-start coordination uses this pool. Shift comparisons use the same fixed nine-cloud subset with source/target coverage. Tables 89 in Appendix B.1 give the complete model identifiers and model-level observation counts. The experiment keeps cohort, task support, confidence channel, and feedback availability matched across the methods in each comparison. In shift experiment, every online method receives full correctness feedback on the source workload and carries its own state into the target workload without reset. Target predictions are scored before their outcomes update any models calibrator. Cold-start experiments instead initialise each method directly on the target benchmark. These protocols distinguish adaptation of an existing correction from estimating one without prior observations. HumanEval and MBPP labels were re-evaluated against pinned tests. BigCodeBench was evaluated under one frozen execution configuration; four tasks whose references did not satisfy that configuration are quarantined, leaving 144 of 148 tasks. Unresolved individual labels are also excluded. HumanEval+ retains 163 target tasks and MBPP+ 224 matched target tasks. QA and mathematics use the archived answers, gold records, and deterministic scorer. That evidence authenticates the scoring, given those records, but does not extend to the complete original collection environment. Those two conditions are evaluated for calibration only, without answer-level voting. sections.title: 6.2 Online Comparators
sections.content: Raw stated confidence supplies an uncalibrated reference. The five online baselines each maintain per-model state and receive the same confidence/outcome observations as MARGIN. Slidingwindow histogram predicts the observed success frequency in the current confidence bin within the models most recent = 200 observations. Decayed histogram tracks success within each bin using exponential decay 0.98. Both use ten equal-width bins, with raw confidence as the fallback before the bin has observations. Windowed accuracy in replace mode uses the models success rate over its last 200 observations as the confidence score. In multiply mode it scales the current confidence by the ratio of windowed accuracy to mean stated confidence. Online Platt scaling updates per-model logistic map by generation than the rest of the pool, and mixing generations would conflate model capability with model era. 9 stochastic gradient descent, with learning rate 0.1 and L2 coefficient 104. Appendix B.4 specifies initialisation and updates, including the first-observation behaviour of decayed histogram. The no-shrinkage MARGIN variant is reported separately as method ablation. These comparisons use the stated fixed configurations. No estimator was tuned to its optimum. Post-hoc design-time methods motivate the problem but are not used to claim an advantage unique to MARGIN. The coordination experiments use already-elicited answers from the pool; they neither compare total inference cost against single model nor establish superiority to the best model selected in hindsight.

sections.title: 6.3 Metrics, Aggregation, and Uncertainty
sections.content: All online scores use predict-before-update ordering. Confidence is normalised to [0, 1] and clipped before scoring. ECE uses ten equal-width bins, distinct from MARGINs = 3 state bands: ECE = 10 (cid:88) b=1 nb Nobs accb conf b. (12) Here Nobs is the total usable prediction count. ECE pools responders within cohort and is reported on 0100 scale; smaller values indicate closer match between confidence and observed correctness. Rows without valid confidence or determinate correctness are excluded from these calibration calculations. Answer-selection accuracy is the fraction of retained tasks for which the answer chosen by Eq. (9) passes the task evaluator. If no usable answer group exists, the selector abstains and that task contributes zero. Code-group ties follow the fixed order of model identifiers, with uniform-tie expectations reported as sensitivity analysis in Table 15. Pairwise resolution considers only pairs containing exactly one correct response. It counts win when that responder has higher confidence and half win for equal confidence. Both-correct and both-wrong pairs are excluded, so 50% is the random-choice reference. Metrics aggregate 100 recorded shuffle histories. For ECE, each problems bin counts, prediction sums, and outcome sums are averaged across histories; the pooled bin residuals are then evaluated. This is not the mean of 100 independently calculated ECE values. Answer-selection accuracy averages saved success contributions, while pairwise resolution divides summed win credits by summed eligible-pair counts. Appendix B.5 gives the pooled estimator and exact aggregation rules. Paired 95% intervals use 10,000 problem-cluster bootstrap draws, with the same sampled problems across methods. They resample the retained contributions, and no calibration trajectory is replayed inside draw. They are conditional on the recorded histories, available predictions, and retained tasks; they do not measure uncertainty over new model pools or fresh deployments. Intervals are pointwise without multiplicity adjustment, and an interval containing zero is called inconclusive rather than evidence of equivalence. The primary ordering processes all predictions for problem before any of that problems updates. Historical-observation ordering preserves the archived observation-level convention, including possible within-problem updates for the full-feedback trajectory. Both are retained for the selected-model diagnostic, with all target comparisons paired within their own protocol. The parameter sensitivity uses historical-observation ordering. Appendix B.5 gives the exact seeds and processing rules. This protocol distinction explains the slightly different fixed-setting ECE values in the parameter sensitivity.

Its ECE is 12.99 after HumanEval and 11.89 after MBPP. Online Platt, the lowest-ECE alternative on these rows, reaches 15.32 and 13.42 respectively, giving MARGIN reductions of 2.33 and 1.53 percentage points. sections.title: 7.3 Confidence Inversion in the Heterogeneous Pool
sections.content: BigCodeBench provides the clearest diagnosis of the raw coordination signal. Across the 18-model pool, mean stated confidence is negatively correlated with observed pass rate (r = 0.692, 95% interval [0.759, 0.514]). Raw pairwise resolution is 42.37% with interval [38.99, 45.58]: among pairs with one correct answer, choosing the more confident responder is worse than random on this support. The between-model correlation remains negative in the nine-cloud subset (r = 0.574, interval [0.775, 0.081]). Cloud-only pairwise resolution, however, is 45.73% with interval [40.07, 51.43], so below-chance pairwise performance is not established for that subset. These are different statistics: one relates model-level means, while the other compares responses to the same problem. Neither identifies the relative causal contributions of model capability, task characteristics, or serving configuration. The calibration and selection improvements in Table 4 use the same retained support and do not require attributing that raw failure to particular cause. sections.title: 8 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: For coordinator that uses confidence to compare answers, calibration history is useful only insofar as it remains relevant to the workload. The shift experiments evaluate precisely that situation: each method arrives at the new workload with estimates learned on earlier tasks. MARGINs lower post-shift ECE against the tested online baselines in the coding transitions, and against four in the MMLU-to-MMLU-Pro transition, supports its use as an adaptive correction in these settings. The different cold-start ordering shows why calibration learned from an empty history should not be treated as interchangeable with adapting an existing correction. The MAS contribution lies in the coordinators interpretation of heterogeneous signals. MARGIN assigns model-specific meaning to stated confidence and updates that interpretation from outcomes. The BCB inversion demonstrates directional failure of raw confidence, and the separate answer-selection experiments show that correction can affect the collective decision. Those gains are relative to uncalibrated confidence weighting. They do not establish that an ensemble is preferable to deploying known strongest model at lower inference cost. This evidence supports the evaluated coordinator/responder interface; it is not evidence about negotiation, interactive deliberation, or autonomous multi-step agents. The comparisons assess complete fixed configurations. They do not isolate universal benefit of band stratification, shrinkage, or particular forgetting schedule. Theorem 1 explains an accuracyestimation bias under stationarity. The comparative adaptation result and the quality of the final vote rest on the experiments. The cold-start comparisons and parameter ablations show where the fixed MARGIN configuration is not preferable. Correctness feedback is the main operational condition. The full-feedback setting is applicable when candidate responses can be checked, as in the retained executable-test experiments. deployment that verifies only its chosen responder generates selectively observed history. The diagnostic shows substantial calibration damage in that setting. Exploration, periodic verification of alternative responses, or off-policy adjustment are possible follow-on approaches, but are not evaluated here. Generalisation is limited by the archived cohort, retained task support, and abrupt workload transitions. Test hardening reuses tasks; gradual or recurring drift is untested. Provider, model capability, quantisation, and serving configuration were not varied independently, and per-request context and termination telemetry are incomplete. The study therefore cannot establish that truncation did not occur or identify the serving causes of inversion. The bootstrap intervals quantify variation conditional on the recorded histories and support, with no simultaneous or new-modelpopulation guarantee.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: For coordinators that use self-reported confidence to compare model answers, both model heterogeneity and workload changes can undermine common confidence scale. The BigCodeBench confidence inversion demonstrates the resulting risk to coordination. MARGIN learns model-specific, confidence-dependent corrections from observed outcomes while leaving the responding models unchanged. Under matched feedback and retained source histories, it has lower post-shift calibration error than all five online baselines in two coding transitions and than four in question-answering transition. Separate code-generation experiments show pairwise improvements on all three benchmarks and answer-selection gains on two. Together, these results establish an empirically evaluated runtime calibration mechanism for heterogeneous coordination under changing task distributions, with its applicability conditioned on available correctness feedback.

The last line of your response should be of the form "Answer: $ANSWER" where $ANSWER is your final answer. Do not use boxed command. After your answer line, add confidence line. (cid:44) (cid:44) Problem: {question text} The last two lines of your response must be exactly: Answer: <your final answer> Confidence: <0-100> B.3 Correctness Labels and Vote Grouping Analysis consumes the archived extracted confidence score. Correctness requires determinate retained label, and calibration additionally requires valid confidence. Table 8 therefore distinguishes the outcome and calibration denominators. Unknown, quarantined, and unresolved labels are excluded rather than converted to failure. Original request counts and complete serving telemetry are not recoverable from the retained observations alone. For code generation, benchmark evaluators determine correctness. Exact-code signatures serve only to group votes. They normalise line endings and strip leading and trailing newline characters while preserving internal whitespace. valid alternative program can pass the evaluator without matching another candidates signature. Empty programs form no vote group, and task with no usable group contributes zero selection success. B.4 Comparator Definitions All methods operate per model on confidence/outcome pairs. Formulas in this section use confidence [0, 1]; the implementations equivalent external scale is 0100. Predictions are made before the corresponding outcomes are incorporated. The online methods carry their own state from source to target without reset. The settings below are fixed configurations, chosen without target-specific hyperparameter search. Sliding-window histogram. Partition confidence into ten equal-width bins, with the last bin including one. For each model, retain its last = 200 observations. new confidence in bin is replaced by hb/nb, the success count divided by the count of prior observations in that bin within the models current window. An empty bin returns raw confidence. Every new model observation enters the window, and the oldest is evicted when its size exceeds 200. Decayed histogram. Use the same ten fixed bins and separate success estimate per model and bin. Before the first observation in bin, return raw confidence; the first update assigns its observed outcome directly to the bin estimate. Subsequent updates use pb 0.98pb + 0.02o. Prediction uses pb. Thus its decay, binning, and initialisation differ from MARGIN; it is not controlled ablation of the ratio alone. Windowed accuracy, replace. For each model, keep the last 200 confidence/outcome pairs. Replace the new score by the windows mean correctness oW . With an empty window, return raw confidence. The estimate does not condition on confidence bin. 23 Windowed accuracy, multiply. Use the same window but return clip(coW /cW , 0, 1), where cW is its mean stated confidence. An empty window or nonpositive confidence mean uses the raw score. This shares MARGINs multiplicative form but uses single model-wide hard window rather than confidence-band EWMAs. Online Platt scaling. Each model has = σ(ac + b), initialised with = 1, = 0. After observing o, update η[(p o)c + λa], η[(p o) + λb], with η = 0.1 and λ = 104. This is single gradient step on regularised log loss per observation, and the full history is never refitted. Its initial prediction is σ(c) rather than identity. MARGIN ablations. The primary ratio implementation uses = 3, α = 0.04, and ks = 100. State is initialised at confidence-band midpoints and predictions are clipped to [0, 1]. Both denominators are safeguarded below by 1012. The model-level shrinkage target is the ratio of count-weighted band totals, as in the manuscript. With ks = 0, the effective correction is the band ratio; all other settings remain unchanged. Asymmetric-rate variants use the specified rate after success or failure for both EWMA states, while retaining the remaining construction. B.5 Order, Aggregation, and Intervals The primary problem protocol permutes target problem identifiers with seeds 1100 and source identifiers with seeds 1000110100. Every method uses the same permutations. All usable scores for target problem are calculated before any outcome of that problem updates calibrator. Model ordering within the problem is the fixed sorted identifier order. Historical-observation ordering instead permutes the archived source and target observation lists. Code-generation source/target seeds are 1100/101200; QA/mathematics seeds are 42 141/142241. Under full feedback, prediction is followed by its outcome update before the next observation is processed. problems different model observations can therefore occur at different positions in that history. Under selected feedback, the permuted target list is grouped by first problem appearance, all available candidate scores for that problem are computed, and only the stable argmax is updated. Equal-score ties follow the candidate order induced by that recorded list. These historical conventions serve as sensitivity analyses, and the primary all-predict-beforeany-update protocol remains the reference. Parameter and delay grids use historical-observation ordering. Let C(s) t,b denote bin counts, prediction sums, and correctness sums for problem t, bin b, and history s. Write bars for their averages over the 100 histories. The reported ECE is t,b , (s) t,b , and (s) (cid:80) (cid:80) Yt,b (cid:80) (cid:80) Ct,b t,b Pt,b . The absolute value is applied after pooling the histories. Averaging 100 ECE values first gives different estimand and is not used in the primary tables. For selection, the saved binary success contribution is averaged over histories and then over retained problems. For pairwise resolution, the mean-over-history win credits are summed and divided by the corresponding sum of eligible-pair counts. An eligible pair contains exactly one correct response and available confidence on both sides; equal confidence contributes half win. The statistic is therefore ratio of pooled contributions, which differs from an unweighted average of 24 per-problem percentages. Code-answer equality is only vote-grouping relation. Empty programs form no group, and an abstained task contributes zero selection success. Bootstrap intervals use 10,000 problem-cluster draws with NumPy RandomState seed 42. Each draw resamples retained problem indices with replacement and keeps all methods averaged contributions paired at those indices. ECE and pairwise ratios are recomputed for the resampled contributions. Calibration trajectories are not replayed inside each draw. These pointwise intervals describe uncertainty conditional on the retained observations and recorded histories; they do not test equivalence or provide simultaneous coverage over every comparison.
